title: India and Oman Just Zeroed Out Tariffs on 98% of Trade. Gulf NRIs Stand to Gain the Most.
excerpt: The India-Oman CEPA came into force on June 1, opening duty-free access across textiles, seafood, gems and 127 services sub-sectors. For the 700,000 Indians in Oman, the agreement reshapes everything from job markets to business opportunities.
body:
The first chilled fish shipment left Chennai airport for Muscat on June 2, less than 24 hours after the India-Oman Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement came into force. It was a modest consignment, but it carried the weight of a deal that opens 98% of bilateral trade to zero tariffs — immediately, not in phases.

The CEPA, signed in December 2025 by Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and Oman's Minister of Commerce Qais bin Mohammed Al Yousef, became operational on June 1. It is the ninth free trade agreement India has signed in three and a half years, and for the roughly 700,000 Indians living and working in Oman, it is arguably the most personally relevant.

## What the Deal Actually Does

Oman has eliminated its 5% most-favored-nation duty on all 945 textile and apparel tariff lines. Immediately. Not over five years, not over ten — now. The same zero-duty access applies to handicrafts, gems and jewellery, agricultural products, and all marine products including shrimp, fish, and cuttlefish.

On the services side, the agreement liberalizes 127 sub-sectors, covering everything from professional consulting to IT services. For Indian professionals working in Oman, this means expanded mobility provisions and a clearer legal framework for cross-border work.

The numbers show the opportunity. India's textile exports to Oman currently stand at $95.1 million against Oman's annual textile imports of $598 million. India holds just 11% of Oman's market and ranks as only its third-largest supplier. With tariff barriers eliminated overnight, Indian exporters can undercut competitors from China, Bangladesh, and Turkey who still face the standard 5% duty.

## Why This Matters in a War Economy

The timing is not coincidental. The CEPA matures against a backdrop of disrupted Gulf shipping lanes, elevated oil prices, and fractured regional supply chains. Oman, positioned at the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz but carefully neutral in the U.S.-Iran conflict, offers India something rare in the current environment: a stable Gulf partner with functioning ports and predictable trade rules.

For India, which sources a significant share of its energy from the Gulf, deepening economic ties with Oman is strategic insurance. Oman's oil and gas exports to India will also benefit from reduced tariffs on petrochemicals and minerals, potentially sweetening the terms on energy supplies at a time when every barrel matters.

The agreement also includes a fully digitalized Certificate of Origin framework — electronic verification between the two countries that reduces paperwork, cuts transaction costs, and eliminates the bureaucratic friction that has historically plagued Indian exporters dealing with Gulf customs.

## The NRI Angle Is the Biggest Story

India's trade agreements rarely get personal. This one does.

Oman hosts one of the oldest Indian diaspora communities in the Gulf. Unlike the massive populations in the UAE or Saudi Arabia, the Indian community in Oman has a distinct character — smaller, more established, with deep roots in trading, retail, construction, and professional services. Many have been there for generations, building businesses that straddle both economies.

The CEPA's services liberalization opens new doors for Indian professionals. Easier cross-border recognition of qualifications, clearer rules for setting up businesses, and expanded visa provisions mean an Indian architect in Muscat or an IT consultant in Salalah now has a treaty-backed framework for their work.

For Indian exporters targeting the Gulf market, Oman becomes the natural entry point. The duty-free access, combined with Oman's relatively simple customs procedures and its Free Trade Agreement with Singapore through the GCC, creates a hub from which Indian goods can reach the wider region.

## The Bigger Picture: India's FTA Blitz

The Oman CEPA is part of a deliberate strategy. India has signed nine FTAs covering 38 economies since 2023, including deals with the UK, New Zealand, and the four-nation EFTA bloc (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein). Commerce Minister Goyal indicated on Friday that six to seven more agreements are expected in the next year, with the first tranche of the U.S. bilateral trade agreement likely by mid-July.

India's export ambitions have outgrown its domestic market. With a $30 trillion global opportunity in front of it — Goyal's phrase — and competitors like Vietnam and Bangladesh aggressively courting the same buyers, India is using trade agreements to lock in preferential access before the window closes.

For NRIs in Oman and the Gulf, this is not abstract trade policy. It is the framework that governs their businesses, their professional mobility, and the cost of goods they buy and sell every day. The first fish may have already landed in Muscat, but the real impact of this deal will unfold over years.

*Sources: Ministry of Commerce and Industry, India Shipping News, The Hindu BusinessLine, Maritime Gateway, Reuters*
